introduction: “I am but a reed”, the opening image suggests: the Manifestation of God does not speak or act of his own volition. He was silent and was made to speak, seated and made to rise, asleep and awakened; he is a straw before the wind; he does not hold the controls of the divine Will; and the last reading asks the believer for a consecration of the same shape. The prophets of Israel said this of themselves: the lion has roared, there is fire in the bones, the Spirit set me on my feet, what the Lord says that will I speak. John’s Jesus says he can do nothing of himself, and the Qur’an that its Prophet does not speak of his own desire. Tagore and Rumi chose the same instrument for their image. Three companions complicate it. Gethsemane lets us hear a will before it is given up; Socrates says that inspired poets are moved in the same way and do not know what they say; and Hobbes observes that from outside inspiration and conviction cannot be told apart.
questions: “Let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will.” Is the Manifestation in these readings without a will of his own, or one whose will is wholly given? Does the difference matter?
Socrates says poets are moved like iron rings by a magnet and do not understand their own words. How do readings 10 to 14 distinguish revelation from that kind of inspiration?
Hobbes says we have only the claimant’s word for it. What, on the readings’ account, lets a hearer judge that a voice is not “mere impulse”?
The last reading asks the believer for a consecration that leaves no trace of self-will. How is what is asked of the believer like, and unlike, what is said of the Manifestation?

outside.why: “From my pen floweth only the summons which Thine own exalted pen hath voiced.” Tagore of himself: this little flute of a reed thou hast carried over hills and dales, and hast breathed through it melodies eternally new.
In John’s Gospel: I have not spoken of myself; but the Father which sent me, he gave me a commandment, what I should say, and what I should speak.
The reading interprets the “reed” of the Apocalypse as a perfect soul, emptied like a reed. Rumi begins his great poem with that instrument: hearken to the reed-flute, how it complains.
He “hath chosen for Himself no will or purpose”. Gethsemane: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt.
The same prayer begins: if it be possible, let this cup pass from me. There a will is heard before it is surrendered. Do the readings describe the absence of a will, or its gift?
The works of the Manifestations “are all ordained by God”. The Son can do nothing of himself, but what he seeth the Father do.
“He was seated — the hands of power and might made Him arise.” Ezekiel: the spirit entered into me when he spake unto me, and set me upon my feet.
“I was silent when the Truth … caused Me to speak.” Amos: the lion hath roared, who will not fear? the Lord God hath spoken, who can but prophesy?
A bit of straw before a great wind, blown as the wind desires. The wind bloweth where it listeth, and thou canst not tell whence it cometh, and whither it goeth.
“I have not penned a single letter … except by Thy leave.” The Qur’an of its Prophet: nor doth he speak of his own desire; it is naught save an inspiration that is inspired.
He “hath spoken not from mere impulse”. David’s last words: the Spirit of the Lord spake by me, and his word was in my tongue.
The apostolic account of all prophecy: it came not in old time by the will of man, but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost.

Hobbes: to say God hath spoken to a man in a dream is no more than to say he dreamed that God spake to him. From outside, “not of my own volition” and strong conviction look the same. How do the readings expect a hearer to tell them apart?
Not a word was recorded except as revealed. Micaiah, urged to prophesy smooth things like the rest: what the Lord saith unto me, that will I speak.
“Think ye … that I hold within My grasp the control of God’s ultimate Will?” Of that day and that hour knoweth no man, no, not the angels, neither the Son, but the Father.

Out of his mouth proceeds only what God has inspired. Socrates tells the reciter Ion that poets too speak not by art but because a divinity moves them, as a magnet moves rings of iron, and adds that they do not understand what they say. What distinguishes the Prophet’s case from the poet’s?
The believer in turn is to be so consecrated that no trace of self-will remains. Dante’s blessed: in His will is our peace.
